stem: Soda-Fountain Wire: Created in Waco in 1885 to smell like an old drugstore counter, every Dr Pepper can proudly boasts [ _____ ].
ahaFactoid: Pharmacist Charles Alderton mixed cherry, almond, licorice, and spice notes—the exact 23-flavor recipe still stays locked in two separate vaults!

stem: Kitchen Vault: Colonel Sanders guarded his Original Recipe fried chicken breading so fiercely that two suppliers separately blend its [ _____ ].
ahaFactoid: Neither Griffith Laboratories nor McCormick knows the full formula—their half-blends only meet at a third plant before hitting KFC fryers!

stem: Scoop Shop Flash: Glendale partners Burt Baskin and Irv Robbins promised a fresh taste for every day of the longest month with [ _____ ].
ahaFactoid: Look closely at Baskin-Robbins’s pink-and-blue "BR" logo—the pink strokes hidden inside the letters literally spell out the number 31!

stem: Medieval English bakers risked stiff fines—or the pillory—for short-weight bread, so they slipped in a spare loaf to form a "baker’s dozen" of how many?
ahaFactoid: King Henry III’s 1266 Assize of Bread punished light loaves harshly, making one extra free roll the cheapest insurance in medieval London!

stem: French Brigade Lore: Tradition says a tall white pleated chef’s toque carries exactly [ _____ ], representing every classic way to cook an egg.
ahaFactoid: Celebrity chef Marie-Antoine Carême popularized the towering hat in the 1800s—the taller the starched crown, the higher your kitchen rank!

stem: Naples Oven Rule: Under strict Vera Pizza Napoletana standards, a blistering wood-fired dome must bake a classic pie in no more than [ _____ ].
ahaFactoid: At roughly 900°F on volcanic brick, dough puffs into leopard-spotted blisters in a minute and a half before its San Marzano sauce can dry out!

stem: Torched golden meringue peaks shielding an icy scoop of vanilla over sponge cake: what flashy banquet dessert survives a blast in a scorching oven?
ahaFactoid: Thousands of tiny air bubbles whipped into egg whites act like oven-mitt insulation, browning outside while keeping the ice cream core frozen solid!

stem: Flambéed tableside with dark rum, butter, and brown sugar at Brennan’s in 1951 New Orleans, which blazing dessert honors a local crime commissioner?
ahaFactoid: New Orleans was America’s booming banana import hub in 1951, so chef Paul Blangé turned surplus fruit into a show-stopping fireball over vanilla!

stem: In 1955, Campbell’s test-kitchen whiz Dorcas Reilly stirred cream of mushroom soup, beans, and crispy fried onions into what Thanksgiving classic?
ahaFactoid: Reilly only had pantry staples most 1950s kitchens already stocked—and her original stained index card now sits proudly in the Inventors Hall of Fame!

stem: Mixing ginger ale, a ruby splash of grenadine, and a maraschino cherry at 1930s Hollywood supper clubs created which beloved zero-proof mocktail?
ahaFactoid: Amusingly, the real child star grew up hating how syrupy-sweet her namesake drink tasted whenever waiters proudly slid one across the table!

stem: Literally translating to "mixed rice" in Korean, which sizzling stone-bowl favorite crowns warm grains with seasoned veggies, chili paste, and an egg?
ahaFactoid: When served in a blazing-hot dolsot stone pot, the bottom layer of rice toasts into crunchy golden nurungji while you stir everything together!

stem: Island Lunchbox: WWII Pacific rations hooked Hawaii so deeply on Hormel’s 1937 canned pork that corner stores wrap sushi-style musubi around [ _____ ].
ahaFactoid: Hawaii consumes more cans of Spam per capita than any other U.S. state—and even McDonald’s locations across the islands serve it at breakfast!

stem: Unlike wheat-flour spaghetti, classic northern Italian gnocchi gets its pillowy, tender bite by kneading flour together with riced what?
ahaFactoid: Cooks roll each dumpling off the tines of a fork to carve tiny ridges that trap butter-sage sauce or rich tomato ragù in every bite!

stem: Before pounding sweet basil, garlic, olive oil, and Parmigiano in a marble mortar for Ligurian pesto, cooks traditionally add which teardrop nuts?
ahaFactoid: Harvested by hand from Mediterranean stone-pine cones, pricey pine nuts explain why authentic jar pesto costs twice as much as marinara!

stem: Stovetop Klaxon! Three of these pantry rules are solid kitchen science, while one stubborn pasta-night habit gets the physics backwards. Spot the myth!
ahaFactoid: Dissolved salt actually nudges water’s boiling point slightly HIGHER—chefs salt pasta water purely so every noodle absorbs flavor from inside out!

stem: Whisking butter, flour, and warm milk with a grating of nutmeg builds which velvety white French mother sauce at the heart of lasagna and mac and cheese?
ahaFactoid: Named after Louis XIV’s chief steward Louis de Béchamel, adding melted Gruyère instantly promotes this silky base into Mornay sauce!

stem: Runny eggs gently poached right inside a bubbling skillet of spiced crushed tomatoes, roasted peppers, and cumin: name this North African brunch star!
ahaFactoid: Derived from Tunisian Arabic slang meaning "all mixed up," shakshuka arrived with New World tomatoes before sweeping cafés from Tel Aviv to Brooklyn!

stem: Blistered, caramelized egg custard baked inside shatteringly crisp pastry shells: Lisbon’s monks perfected which famed Portuguese tart from leftover yolks?
ahaFactoid: Jerónimos Monastery monks starched their robes with egg whites—turning leftover golden yolks into Lisbon’s sweetest culinary icon in 1837!

stem: Literally Italian for "drowned," what effortless two-ingredient cafe treat pours a piping-hot shot of espresso straight over cold vanilla gelato?
ahaFactoid: The contrast of bitter boiling espresso melting sweet fior di latte cream delivers dessert and after-dinner coffee in one glorious chilled glass!

stem: Griddled golden cornmeal rounds sliced open like warm pockets and packed with melty cheese or slow-braised beef: which street food unites Colombia and Venezuela?
ahaFactoid: Indigenous cooks ground maize into arepas long before Columbus arrived—today pre-cooked Harina P.A.N. turns out crispy rounds in ten minutes flat!

stem: Ski-Lodge Craze: Promoted in the 1930s by a Swiss dairy cartel desperate to move winter Gruyère, bubbling caquelon-pot [ _____ ] conquered 1960s dinner parties.
ahaFactoid: The Swiss Cheese Union coined the slogan "Fondue is good and creates a good mood"—and by 1966 every hip suburban host owned long color-coded forks!

stem: Finely chopped parsley, oregano, garlic, chili flakes, and zippy red-wine vinegar unite in which bright green Argentine sauce spooned over grilled steak?
ahaFactoid: Unlike Italian pesto, authentic chimichurri is chopped by knife rather than pureed smooth—and folklore even traces its name to Basque "tximitxurri"!

stem: Simmering toasted chilis, warm spices, sesame seeds, and a bold square of unsweetened chocolate builds which glossy dark Mexican sauce famed in Puebla?
ahaFactoid: From Nahuatl "mōlli" (sauce), a master Puebla mole layers 20+ ingredients so chocolate lends deep, velvety complexity—never candy sweetness!

stem: Fluted cast-aluminum ring with a central chimney that bakes thick batters evenly: what Minneapolis cake mold exploded after a 1966 Pillsbury Bake-Off?
ahaFactoid: Nordic Ware barely sold any Bundt pans until Ella Helfrich’s gooey "Tunnel of Fudge" took second place in 1966—sparking 200,000 mail-in requests overnight!

stem: Conical clay chimney perched over a shallow glazed dish so rising steam condenses and drips back onto spiced lamb: name this water-saving North African pot!
ahaFactoid: Engineered for arid regions where every drop of water counted, the peaked lid acts like a self-basting dome that turns tough cuts butter-tender!

stem: Deli Board: Piling warm corned beef, tangy sauerkraut, melted Swiss, and Russian dressing onto butter-griddled rye builds an unmistakable [ _____ ].
ahaFactoid: Both Omaha’s Blackstone Hotel poker games and Arnold Reuben’s NYC deli claim the 1920s creation—either way, it won the 1956 Sandwich Prize!

stem: Bayou Pot: Borrowing its name from the West African Bantu word "ki ngombo" for okra, Louisiana’s rich dark-roux stew [ _____ ] is ladled over warm rice.
ahaFactoid: Great gumbo cooks stir flour and oil for forty straight minutes until the roux hits milk-chocolate brown—stop stirring for ten seconds and you start over!

stem: Dessert Torch: Translating literally to "burnt cream," chilled vanilla custard beneath a shatteringly crisp sheet of caramelized sugar is called [ _____ ].
ahaFactoid: First printed in François Massialot’s 1691 cookbook, its signature tabletop thrill is cracking that glossy sugar crust cleanly with the back of your spoon!

stem: Blending peak-summer tomatoes, cucumber, garlic, olive oil, and day-old bread served icy cold from a pitcher yields which refreshing Andalusian soup?
ahaFactoid: Before tomatoes crossed the Atlantic, Spanish farmhands already pounded stale bread, garlic, vinegar, and olive oil to beat 100°F heat!

stem: Among more than 25,000 orchid species blooming on Earth, America’s most popular ice-cream flavor comes from the cured seed pod of which lone edible crop?
ahaFactoid: Because each vanilla blossom opens for just one single morning, 12-year-old enslaved boy Edmond Albius invented hand-pollination in 1841—still used today!

stem: How does papery-thin Italian prosciutto crudo differ from baked deli ham? It is never cooked or smoked—just patiently cured with sea salt and what?
ahaFactoid: Parma’s curing houses open tall shuttered windows to let fragrant Apennine breezes slowly dry hanging hams for one to two full years!

stem: Diner Klaxon! Three of these snack-aisle truths are 100% documented science, while one fiery chili warning misses the mark. Spot the myth!
ahaFactoid: Capsaicin merely hijacks heat-sensing TRPV1 pain nerves to shout "fire!"—zero real tissue burn occurs, though milk’s casein washes the oil away fast!

stem: Coffeehouse Klaxon! Three of these barista facts check out with café pros, while one morning-mug assumption gets it flipped backwards. Catch the myth!
ahaFactoid: Dark roasting puffs beans larger and cooks oils smoky without adding caffeine—measured by scoop, dense light roasts actually deliver slightly MORE buzz!

stem: Goan cooks took Portuguese sailors’ wine-and-garlic pork stew ("vinha d’alhos") and added fiery palm vinegar and chilis to invent which tangy curry?
ahaFactoid: Even though takeout spots toss in spuds ("aloo" means potato in Hindi), traditional Goan vindaloo had zero potatoes—just wine, garlic, and fire!

stem: Honoring a pockmarked Chengdu grandmother who fed hungry oil porters in 1862, which tingling Sichuan dish marries silky bean curd with fermented chili beans?
ahaFactoid: Its signature electric buzz ("málà") comes from Sichuan peppercorns—citrus-family husks that make your tongue literally vibrate at 50 Hertz!

stem: Those salty olive-green pops scattered atop lox bagels and chicken piccata aren’t miniature berries at all—capers are actually pickled unopened what?
ahaFactoid: Picked by hand at dawn off prickly Mediterranean bushes before they bloom into purple-white blossoms, the tiniest "non-pareil" buds fetch top dollar!

stem: Wrapping seared beef tenderloin in savory chopped mushroom duxelles, prosciutto, and golden puff pastry creates which showstopping British banquet roast?
ahaFactoid: Chefs brush crepe or prosciutto around the meat like a waterproof raincoat so mushroom moisture never turns that flaky puff-pastry crust soggy!

stem: Holiday Table Klaxon! Three of these food facts hold up in nutrition labs, while one classic Thanksgiving excuse is a sleepy tall tale. Spot the myth!
choices: Pears ripen best off the tree
ahaFactoid: Chicken breast and cheddar pack just as much tryptophan per ounce—Thanksgiving couch naps are really caused by massive mounds of stuffing, pie, and wine!

stem: Bistro Klaxon! Three of these culinary oddities are 100% real, while one viral guacamole-saving trick does almost nothing. Call out the myth!
ahaFactoid: The pit only protects the tiny circle directly beneath it by blocking air—pressing plastic wrap flush onto the guacamole stops browning way better!

stem: Japanese cooks adapted lacy ice-cold batter frying in the 1500s from Portuguese Jesuits’ meatless Lenten days ("quattuor tempora"), creating what dish?
ahaFactoid: Mixing icy water lightly into flour keeps gluten from forming, so battered shrimp puffs into a featherlight crisp halo in seconds of hot sesame oil!

stem: NBA Wire, March 1962: Inside a half-full arena in Hershey, Pennsylvania, Philadelphia titan Wilt Chamberlain dropped a single-game [ _____ ] on the Knicks!
ahaFactoid: Zero TV cameras taped the night! Chamberlain—a career 51% foul shooter—miraculously sank 28 of 32 underhand free throws to hit the century mark!

stem: Hoops Rescue, 1954: Sick of teams stalling into 19-18 snoozers, Syracuse owner Danny Biasone saved pro basketball by inventing the [ _____ ] shot clock.
ahaFactoid: Biasone divided 2,880 game seconds by 120 lively shots to land on 24—and NBA scoring immediately jumped 14 points per team overnight!

stem: Links Ledger: After Scotland’s Old Course at St. Andrews trimmed its seaside loop from 22 in 1764, a standard round of golf settled forever at [ _____ ].
ahaFactoid: Early golfers played out-and-back over the exact same fairways—once St. Andrews merged four short holes into two, every club on Earth copied 18!

stem: Diamond Wire, 1941: From May 15 to July 16, Yankee Clipper Joe DiMaggio enthralled radio listeners across America with baseball’s iconic [ _____ ] hit streak!
ahaFactoid: The night after Cleveland third baseman Ken Keltner finally robbed him to end it, DiMaggio calmly started ANOTHER 16-game hitting streak!

stem: After 1930s pros started forcing poor caddies to lug 25-iron trunks around courses, golf’s rulemakers capped every tournament bag at how many clubs?
ahaFactoid: Pack one extra wedge by mistake and you get docked two penalty strokes per hole—Ian Woosnam infamously lost the 2001 Open Championship that exact way!

stem: Every official Major League baseball is still stitched completely by hand with waxed red cotton thread forming exactly how many raised double stitches?
ahaFactoid: Those 108 raised seams aren’t decoration—pitchers grip them to spin curveballs and sliders by grabbing turbulent air at 95 mph!

stem: Blasting career homer #715 over Atlanta’s left-field wall on April 8, 1974, which Braves slugger finally broke Babe Ruth’s legendary 39-year record?
ahaFactoid: Even if you erased every single one of Hammerin’ Hank’s 755 home runs, he STILL collected over 3,000 career base hits!

stem: Calling himself "the luckiest man on the face of the earth" at Yankee Stadium in 1939, which "Iron Horse" played 2,130 consecutive MLB games?
ahaFactoid: Gehrig’s famous streak began by chance in June 1925 when regular first baseman Wally Pipp sat out with a headache—making "getting Pipped" sports slang!

stem: Sprinting full-tilt away from home plate in the 1954 World Series to glove Vic Wertz’s 425-foot drive over his shoulder: who pulled off "The Catch"?
ahaFactoid: Even crazier than the over-the-shoulder grab? Mays spun on a dime and fired a rocket back to the infield to hold the runner from scoring!

stem: Walking into the 1988 NBA Three-Point Contest locker room to ask rivals "Who’s coming in second?" before winning in his warmup jacket: who backed it up?
ahaFactoid: Bird raised one index finger toward the ceiling before his final money ball even swished through the net—claiming his third straight shootout crown!

stem: Having BOTH #8 and #24 retired by the Lakers and pouring in 81 points against Toronto in 2006, which relentless guard called himself the "Black Mamba"?
ahaFactoid: Bryant remains the only player in NBA history to earn two separate jersey retirements with the same franchise—winning five rings across two decades!

stem: Racking up a staggering 14 French Open trophies and a 112-4 mark on Paris’s crushed red brick dust, which Spanish left-hander ruled as "King of Clay"?
ahaFactoid: Naturally right-handed in daily life, young Rafa switched to a vicious left-handed forehand whip whose heavy topspin bounced right over rivals’ shoulders!

stem: Relaxing poolside in Miami in January 1969, which fur-coat-wearing Jets quarterback boldly guaranteed—and pulled off—an 18-point Super Bowl III upset?
ahaFactoid: Namath’s 16-7 win over Baltimore proved the upstart AFL could hang with the mighty NFL—and famously wagged his #1 finger running down the tunnel!

stem: Lanes Tradition: Because 1800s Thanksgiving alleys awarded holiday birds to hot rollers, stringing three consecutive bowling strikes is still cheered as a [ _____ ].
ahaFactoid: Back when bowling pins were hand-set and alleys were crooked timber, three strikes in a row was rare enough to earn Sunday’s whole feast!

stem: In tennis, when a zipping serve clips the top white tape of the net yet still drops cleanly inside the proper service box, what call grants a free do-over?
ahaFactoid: From old English "let" meaning "hindrance"—tiny sensors clipped inside the net cord now beep umpires the instant a serve clips the tape!

stem: Dugout Klaxon! Three of these real-world sports truths hold up in every rulebook, while one classic sandlot belief gets called out. Catch the myth!
choices: Tie games count in NFL records
ahaFactoid: Inside-the-park home runs count every bit as much—Roberto Clemente even smacked a walk-off inside-the-park GRAND SLAM in 1956!

stem: Striding onto Centre Court in crisp cream blazers while claiming a men’s-record eight Wimbledon singles titles, which Swiss star became grass-court royalty?
ahaFactoid: Federer even went five straight Wimbledons without losing a match from 2003 to 2007—and played the epic 2008 dusk final hailed as tennis’s greatest duel!

stem: After heading in two goals to crown France at the 1998 World Cup, which velvet-footed midfielder ended his 2006 Final career with a shocking red-card headbutt?
ahaFactoid: Minutes before his stunning exit in Berlin, Zidane had coolly chipped a Panenka penalty off the bar—walking right past the gold trophy!

stem: Sweeping all four tennis Grand Slams PLUS Olympic singles gold inside the single calendar year of 1988, who completed the sport’s lone Golden Slam?
ahaFactoid: At age 19, Graf even double-bageled Natasha Zvereva 6-0, 6-0 in 34 minutes in that year’s French Open final before capturing gold in Seoul!

stem: Rink Folklore: Tallying one goal, one assist, and dropping the gloves for one five-minute fight in the same hockey game is cheered as a [ _____ ] hat trick.
ahaFactoid: Amusingly, "Mr. Hockey" only logged that exact combo TWICE in his 32-year career—Rick Tocchet holds the NHL record with 18!

stem: Soaring completely horizontal in midair with arms raised after scoring Boston’s 1970 Stanley Cup overtime clincher: who stars in hockey’s greatest photo?
ahaFactoid: St. Louis defender Noel Picard tripped Orr the split-second he fired past Glenn Hall—launching the defenseman into a bronze statue outside TD Garden!

stem: Charging up brutal California hills every offseason on his way to 22,895 receiving yards and 208 touchdowns, who towers atop NFL receiver history?
ahaFactoid: Rice’s lead is so absurd that if you took away his first FIVE NFL seasons, his remaining yardage would STILL rank inside the top ten all-time!

stem: Nicknamed "Sweetness" for both his graceful jukes and generous spirit, which Bears running back lends his name to the NFL’s Man of the Year award?
ahaFactoid: Payton missed just ONE game in 13 bruising seasons—and every winner of his namesake honor wears a permanent silhouetted jersey patch!

stem: Beating childhood polio and heavy leg braces to sweep the 100m, 200m, and 4x100m relay at the 1960 Rome Olympics, who sprinted into TV history?
ahaFactoid: Home in Clarksville, Tennessee as "the fastest woman in the world," Rudolph insisted her victory parade and banquet be fully integrated!

stem: Sticking consecutive perfect-10 vaults at the 1984 Los Angeles Games to become America’s first women’s Olympic all-around gymnastics champ: who leaped to gold?
ahaFactoid: Needing a flawless 10 on her final apparatus to edge Ecaterina Szabo by 0.05, Retton clinched on Vault #1—then stuck a second 10 anyway!

stem: Frantic brooms sweeping pebbled ice ahead of a 42-pound polished Scottish granite rock gliding toward a bullseye called "the button": name this Olympic sport!
ahaFactoid: Every single Olympic curling stone on Earth is quarried from rare water-repellent granite on one tiny uninhabited Scottish island—Ailsa Craig!

stem: Named after an English seed merchant who donated its gleaming gold chalice in 1927, which biennial match-play clash pits Team USA against Team Europe?
ahaFactoid: Samuel Ryder made his fortune selling penny seed packets—and golfers play the event purely for team pride with zero official prize money!

stem: When a full-strength NHL squad blasts the puck from behind center red all the way past the rival goal line untouched, linesmen whistle play dead for what?
ahaFactoid: To punish stalling, the offending squad cannot swap tired skaters before the faceoff—though shorthanded penalty killers get a free pass!

stem: In Formula 1 and IndyCar, why is the quickest qualifier starting up front on the grid said to hold "pole position"? The phrase came straight from which sport?
ahaFactoid: On oval dirt racetracks, the inside rail beside the starting distance pole gave horses the shortest path around every turn—and motorsport kept the phrase!

stem: Playoff games grind on until someone scores—but if a regular-season NFL overtime game stays deadlocked when the extra 10-minute clock hits 0:00, what happens?
ahaFactoid: Several stunned NFL pros—including Donovan McNabb in 2008—confessed on live TV they had no idea regular-season games could even end tied!

stem: Olympic Klaxon! Three of these wild Games milestones actually happened, while one famous fiery ritual is way younger than you think. Spot the myth!
choices: Early Games held live art events
ahaFactoid: Ancient Olympia kept a stationary sacred altar flame with ZERO cross-country relay—the modern Olympic torch relay was invented for the 1936 Berlin Games!

stem: Hardwood & Diamond Klaxon! Three of these Hall-of-Fame stats are 100% legit, while one towering record claim gets whistled for a foul. Catch the myth!
choices: Babe Ruth began as a pitcher
Wilt fouled out twice in NBA
ahaFactoid: Across 1,045 regular-season games and 160 playoff battles, Wilt Chamberlain NEVER fouled out a single time—zero ejections on six fouls in his whole career!

stem: Gliding down Rome’s cobblestone Appian Way completely barefoot to win the 1960 Olympic marathon in world-record time: which Ethiopian hero stunned the globe?
ahaFactoid: Bikila ditched his sponsor’s blister-giving shoes hours before the start—then came back four years later in Tokyo wearing sneakers to win gold AGAIN!

stem: Mexico City Wire, 1968: Soaring 29 feet 2.5 inches in crisp high-altitude air, [ _____ ] shattered the Olympic long-jump mark by nearly two full feet!
ahaFactoid: Beamon soared clean past the stadium’s optical measuring rail—officials had to fetch a humble steel tape measure while he collapsed in shock!

stem: To stop crafty defenders from deliberately dropping easy pop-ups to spark cheap double plays with runners on first and second, umps invoke which rule?
ahaFactoid: Added in 1895 after slick Baltimore Orioles fielders kept baiting trapped baserunners, the batter is called out automatically while the ball stays live!

stem: Gleaming silver wine ewer engraved with champions since 1873 and hoisted each July on breezy British links: what prize crowns The Open Championship?
ahaFactoid: Golf originally awarded a red Morocco-leather Championship Belt—until Young Tom Morris won it three times straight in 1870 and got to keep it forever!

stem: Crowned by a cork nose and exactly 16 left-wing goose feathers that rocket off strings past 300 mph before braking dramatically: name this feathered flyer!
ahaFactoid: No matter how awkwardly a shuttlecock gets smashed, its cork tip always flips forward in midair so the feathered skirt trails cleanly like a dart!

stem: In cricket, walking back to the pavilion dismissed for zero runs is teasingly called a "duck" because the oval digit 0 on scorebooks resembles what?
ahaFactoid: Getting dismissed on the very first ball you face earns the even crueler honor of a "Golden Duck"—and twice in one match makes a "pair"!

stem: Referee Klaxon! Three of these official rulebook quirks are 100% legal plays, while one shouted sideline claim gets waved off. Spot the myth!
choices: Goalies can score in NHL games
A safety awards two NFL points
ahaFactoid: Under FIFA’s Laws of the Game, a striker can stand right beside the rival keeper on a throw-in, goal kick, or corner—offside NEVER applies directly!

stem: After cleanly fielding a punt, an NFL team may attempt an unguarded free field goal straight from that spot using which ultra-rare rulebook gem?
ahaFactoid: Going nearly half a century between successes from 1976 until the Chargers nailed a 57-yarder in December 2024, it’s football’s rarest three-pointer!

stem: Post Office Flash, 1966: Dropping a one-ounce letter into a blue U.S. mailbox during our broadcast’s home year cost a tiny [ _____ ]!
ahaFactoid: Featuring George Washington’s profile, the 5-cent stamp held steady from 1963 through 1967—today’s first-class stamp runs roughly fifteen times higher!

stem: Corner-Store Legend: Pre-printed straight onto its tall cherry-blossom can since 1992, AriZona Iced Tea fiercely defends its [ _____ ] tag.
ahaFactoid: Founder Don Vultaggio skipped pricey TV ads and thinned cans to keep them under a buck for decades—calling it his thank-you to loyal fans!

stem: When Ray Kroc opened his first franchised McDonald’s in Des Plaines, Illinois in 1955, a freshly griddled hamburger lit up the signboard at how much?
ahaFactoid: You could pair that 15-cent burger with 10-cent fries and a 20-cent milkshake—an entire Friday-night drive-in feast with change back from half a dollar!

stem: Fill ’Er Up, 1966: Pulling a shiny coupe into an American service station in 1966 cost an average of roughly [ _____ ] for a gallon of regular gas!
ahaFactoid: Better still, a uniformed attendant pumped it for you, washed your windshield, checked the oil, and often handed out free drinking glasses or road maps!

stem: Stadium Stub, 1967: Over 30,000 Los Angeles Coliseum seats still sat empty at Super Bowl I even though the most expensive ticket ran just [ _____ ]!
ahaFactoid: Fans grumbled $12 felt steep compared to regular $5 NFL seats—a wild bargain next to modern Super Bowl stubs averaging thousands of dollars apiece!

stem: Unveiled at the 1964 New York World’s Fair to wild showroom crowds, Ford’s brand-new base hardtop Mustang carried a famous sticker price right at what?
ahaFactoid: Ford hoped to move 100,000 Mustangs in Year One—instead, that sporty under-$2,400 tag sold 22,000 cars on Day One and over 400,000 in twelve months!

stem: When an incoming CEO floated raising the $1.50 food-court hot dog combo, co-founder Jim Sinegal famously barked "I will kill you" at which club?
ahaFactoid: Held at $1.50 since 1985, Costco even built its own hot-dog factories in California and Illinois just to keep that famous quarter-pound frank affordable!

stem: Bargain Wire, 2021: Ending 35 years of pricing every single item on its shelves at one exact buck, discount giant [ _____ ] shifted its baseline to $1.25.
ahaFactoid: Shoppers jokingly renamed it "Dollar-Twenty-Five Tree" overnight, though the chain kept its classic green marquee and added $3-$5 Plus aisles!

stem: Which blue-and-yellow furniture maze parks cheap meatballs and $1 soft-serve cones right by checkout so shoppers walk out humming about low prices?
ahaFactoid: Founder Ingvar Kamprad insisted "it’s tough to do business on an empty stomach"—and psychologists proved cheap exit treats sweeten your whole price memory!

stem: Jingle Flash, 2008: One impossibly sticky Miami franchisee promo turned "$5 Footlong" into a multi-billion-dollar national craze for [ _____ ].
ahaFactoid: Franchisee Stuart Frankel started the slow-weekend deal in 2003—five years later its five-note jingle had fans singing down every line!

stem: Handing out basic apps or streaming tiers for $0 while charging superfans for ad-free perks or power-ups earned what catchy 2006 pricing portmanteau?
ahaFactoid: Venture investor Fred Wilson invited blog readers to name the model in 2006—and Jarid Lukin’s snappy mashup of "free" and "premium" stuck immediately!

stem: Dog-eared pocket price guide tucked in dealership desks since 1926 that tells used-car shoppers whether a sedan’s sticker is fair or robbery: name it!
ahaFactoid: Los Angeles dealer Les Kelley first circulated mimeographed sheets listing what he’d pay for Ford Model Ts—and rivals started begging for copies!

stem: Golden, garlicky, and gleaming hot under amber supermarket lamps for $4.99 even when raw poultry costs more: what savory magnet pulls you through the store?
ahaFactoid: Placed deliberately at the far rear of the market, one juicy $4.99 bird routinely leads shoppers to toss $40 of sides, salad, and wine into the cart!

stem: Hollywood studios take the bulk of opening-weekend ticket sales, so movie theaters actually stay afloat on 85%-margin concession markups led by what?
ahaFactoid: Posh 1920s movie palaces first banned smelly popcorn—until Depression slumps forced owners to wheel golden kettles straight into the lobby!

stem: Showroom Slang: Coined in the inflationary late 1970s when car shoppers froze stiff reading dealership window tags, sudden price paralysis is called [ _____ ].
ahaFactoid: Before federal Monroney window labels became law in 1958, car lots didn’t even post clear retail prices—salesmen simply sized up your suit and guessed!

stem: Checkout Klaxon! Three of these real supermarket secrets are true retail tactics, while one confident car-lot boast actually backfires today. Spot the myth!
choices: Kids’ cereals sit at eye level
ahaFactoid: Modern dealerships earn big reserve commissions from auto lenders—so announcing "I’m paying cash" can actually shrink the discount a manager offers!

stem: Red-and-gold storefront signs, polished wooden counters, and lunch stools selling 10-cent treasures across 1960s Main Streets: which chain ruled the five-and-dime?
ahaFactoid: Frank Woolworth’s first 5-cent Utica shop flopped—until adding 10-cent goods in Lancaster funded Manhattan’s soaring Woolworth Building!

stem: Stores advertise ultra-cheap "first 20 shoppers at 5 AM" televisions to spark pre-dawn sidewalk stampedes—what explosive nickname labels those headline deals?
ahaFactoid: Even if twenty TVs vanish in thirty seconds, hundreds of chilly folks already inside the warm store stay to buy full-margin holiday gifts!

stem: Born during the 1930s so cash-strapped shoppers could hold a winter coat via small weekly installments before carrying it home, what store system is this?
ahaFactoid: Unlike credit cards, classic layaway charged zero interest—retailers simply tucked your boxed coat into the back room until your final dime cleared!

stem: Electronics chains love flashing "$50 OFF!" while secretly counting on "slippage"—shoppers forgetting to clip box barcodes and mail forms—via what clunky offer?
ahaFactoid: Studies show 40% to 60% of mail-in rebates never get claimed—letting brands advertise eye-popping prices while pocketing full retail cash!

stem: To keep late-night gamblers from wandering off property for supper, El Rancho Vegas launched a $1 "Buckaroo" spread in 1946—popularizing what dining format?
ahaFactoid: Publicist Herb McDonald stacked cold cuts, salads, and warm roast on a long table for one silver dollar—making the all-you-can-eat buffet a Vegas icon!

stem: To fill quiet restaurant booths at 4:30 PM before the evening rush arrives, diners across America—especially sunny Florida—invented which pre-sunset bargain?
ahaFactoid: Just like off-peak plane seats, empty 4:45 PM tables earn zero—so slinging discounted turkey early lets diners turn every booth twice!

stem: Decades before bars slashed cocktail tabs at 5 PM, U.S. Navy sailors in the 1910s coined which upbeat two-word name for weekly onboard music and boxing breaks?
ahaFactoid: Aboard the USS Arkansas in 1913, "Happy Hour Socials" featured ragtime bands—then Prohibition speakeasies swiped the name for drinks!

stem: Bottled from surplus California vineyards in 2002 and sold exclusively at Trader Joe’s for $1.99, which wine earned the affectionate nickname "Two-Buck Chuck"?
ahaFactoid: Wine snobs laughed until Charles Shaw’s 2005 Chardonnay beat 2,300 rivals in a blind tasting at the California State Fair—selling over a billion bottles!

stem: Packaged with "adoption papers" at $25 retail in December 1983, which yarn-haired dolls ignited department-store scrambles and $200 black-market resale tags?
ahaFactoid: Each doll’s randomized face, hair, and middle name made every box feel one-of-a-kind—triggering a holiday frenzy that made front-page news nationwide!

stem: Bypassing sluggish store shelves in the 1950s and 1960s, sales pioneer Brownie Wise built a suburban empire demonstrating burp-sealed bowls at what home events?
ahaFactoid: Shoppers couldn’t tell how Earl Tupper’s airtight seals worked on a store shelf—so Wise turned living-room demos into a suburban empire!

stem: Daily-Deal Wire: Pooling local buyers for half-off spa and bakery vouchers in 2008, Chicago startup [ _____ ] famously turned down a $6 billion Google buyout!
ahaFactoid: Shops soon realized deal-hunters rarely returned at full price—and Groupon’s stock later fell to a tiny fraction of Google’s rejected bid!

stem: Three gleaming brass spheres hanging outside storefronts since Renaissance bankers lent cash against heirloom watches: which quick-loan shop flies this emblem?
ahaFactoid: Legend links the three golden orbs either to Florence’s Medici crest or St. Nicholas tossing three bags of gold through a poor family’s window!

stem: Comparing a tall "Family Size" cereal box beside a regular one, which tiny corner figure on the grocery shelf label reveals which truly costs less per ounce?
ahaFactoid: Savvy shoppers swear by unit pricing—surprisingly often, a "value pack" actually costs MORE per ounce than grabbing two standard sale-priced boxes!

stem: Browsing wedding bands, a jeweler sets 14-karat beside pure 24-karat gold: why is pricier 24K gold rarely recommended for an everyday ring?
ahaFactoid: Pure 24K gold is malleable enough to dent against a doorknob—blending it with copper or silver into 14K or 18K keeps prongs gripping your diamond tight!

stem: Grocery chains place blooming flowers and warm bakery smells right inside the automatic front doors—instead of bleach—deliberately to spark what habit?
ahaFactoid: Store architects call it the "decompression zone"—warm aromas drop your guard, slow your stride, and nudge you into leisurely browsing every aisle!

stem: Menu Klaxon! Three of these sneaky restaurant-pricing tricks are real menu engineering, while one diner guess misses the math wildly. Catch the myth!
ahaFactoid: Fountain syrup, tap water, and ice cost restaurants mere pennies a glass—even with free refills, fountain drinks are the highest-margin item on the menu!

stem: Price-Tag Klaxon! Three of these jaw-dropping retail comparisons are 100% real, while one nostalgic 1966 living-room claim is way too cheap. Spot the myth!
ahaFactoid: A 1966 RCA walnut-cabinet color TV ran $500 to $700—over $5,000 in today’s dollars, which is why whole neighborhoods gathered at one lucky house on Sunday!

stem: Receipt Klaxon! Three of these bygone price tags are historical fact, while one famous gadget launch price got misremembered way too low. Catch the fake!
ahaFactoid: Steve Jobs launched the 2007 iPhone at $499 (4GB) and $599 (8GB) WITH a 2-year contract—the $199 price didn’t arrive until iPhone 3G!

stem: Inside Sotheby’s or Christie’s auction rooms, the final winning bid shouted right before the gavel slams down—before house fees—is officially called what?
ahaFactoid: Keep your paddle calm! Once the auctioneer calls the hammer price, a 15% to 27% "buyer’s premium" gets stacked right on top of the final invoice!

stem: On eBay or at classic-car auction blocks, what confidential minimum dollar floor protects a nervous seller from letting a prized item walk away for pennies?
ahaFactoid: If bidding stalls short of the seller’s secret reserve, the auctioneer announces "bought in" and the treasure rolls straight back offstage unsold!

stem: Named after a legendary royal gift of sacred albino beasts too expensive to feed, what playful label tags a charity rummage sale or cheeky gag-gift swap?
ahaFactoid: In legend, Siam’s king gifted rare white elephants to rival courtiers—honoring them so richly they couldn’t refuse, yet bankrupting them on hay bills!

stem: Yard-Sale Jackpot: A collector paid $4 at a 1989 Pennsylvania flea market for a gloomy frame—and peeled the backing to discover a $2.4M [ _____ ]!
ahaFactoid: Hidden behind a dull country print sat one of 24 surviving 1776 Dunlap broadside printings of the Declaration—later resold for $8.1M!

stem: Designer "factory outlet" sweaters carry friendlier tags than flagship stores—often not because they’re leftover mall stock, but because brands deliberately do what?
ahaFactoid: Check the label for tiny extra dots, diamonds, or "Factory" stamps—retailers estimate over 80% of outlet-mall apparel is purpose-made at lower fabric cost!

stem: Travel-Hack Klaxon! Three of these real-world pricing secrets check out, while one viral browser trick fails every consumer lab test. Spot the myth!
ahaFactoid: Independent studies checked thousands of searches and found zero secret cookie-hike penalty—fares jump simply when the cheapest seat bucket sells out!

stem: Party Paradox: Gather just [ _____ ] in any room and the mathematical odds that at least two share the exact same birthday already tip past 50%!
ahaFactoid: Your brain checks matches only against YOUR birthday—yet 23 guests create 253 distinct head-to-head pairs, pushing shared-cake odds to 50.7%!

stem: Neatly mirroring the weeks of a calendar year across four seasonal suits, a standard bridge or poker deck (minus Jokers) holds exactly how many cards?
ahaFactoid: Wait till you add all the face values (Ace=1 through King=13) across all four suits plus one Joker: 364 + 1 = 365 days in a year!

stem: Grandmaster Grid: Alternating 32 light tiles and 32 dark tiles across an eight-by-eight battlefield, a classic chess or checkerboard contains [ _____ ].
ahaFactoid: In legend, doubling one grain of rice across all 64 squares creates 18 quintillion grains—more rice than humanity has harvested in all recorded history!

stem: Vegas Wheel: Numbered 1 through 36 plus green 0 and double-zero 00, a standard American roulette wheel splits its spinning bowl into exactly [ _____ ].
ahaFactoid: Single-number bets still pay 35-to-1 as if there were 36 pockets—those two innocent green zero slots hand Las Vegas a tidy 5.26% house edge!

stem: Passing GO, Jail, Free Parking, and Boardwalk, one complete lap around a classic Monopoly board takes your silver top hat across how many spaces?
ahaFactoid: Because Jail draws so much foot traffic, Markov-chain math crowns the Orange street trio (6, 8, and 9 steps from Jail) the board’s stealth money-makers!

stem: Tabletop Count: Running from double-blank all the way up to double-six without repeats, a standard pocket set of dominoes contains exactly [ _____ ].
ahaFactoid: That’s the triangular sum 7 + 6 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 28—and if you line up every tile end-to-end, all 28 close into one unbroken loop!

stem: Running Ten, Jack, Queen, King, and Ace all in one matching suit—beating 649,739 other five-card combos—what unbeatable hand reigns atop poker?
ahaFactoid: Out of 2,598,960 possible five-card deals, literally only FOUR hands in the whole universe are royal flushes—one for hearts, spades, clubs, and diamonds!

stem: Tapping the felt for one greedy extra blackjack card and sailing past 21 immediately forfeits your chips—what blunt phrase names that heartbreak?
ahaFactoid: Even if the dealer ALSO busts thirty seconds later, the casino keeps your chips anyway—that "player busts first" rule is the house’s main edge in 21!

stem: Felt Wire: Once opening Texas Hold’em bets settle, the dealer burns one card face-down and deals three shared community cards together called [ _____ ].
ahaFactoid: Wait until you see how brutal Hold’em math is: holding two unpaired hole cards, you miss pairing anything on the Flop nearly two-thirds of the time!

stem: A quick glance toward your chip stack, shaky hands, or a twitchy eyebrow: what crisp phrase names an unconscious giveaway at the card table?
ahaFactoid: Ironically, pros note that shaky hands at a card table usually signal a MONSTER hand—pure adrenaline from excitement, not bluffing nerves!

stem: Six colorful guests, six miniature metal weapons, and nine mansion rooms tucked inside a confidential yellow envelope: what game turns 324 combos into a whodunit?
ahaFactoid: Invented by bored British musician Anthony Pratt during WWII air-raid blackouts, the prototype was originally titled "Murder!" with a poison vial and axe!

stem: Hexagonal island of sheep, brick, and wheat where rolling two dice’s most frequent sum—a 7—unleashes a sneaky gray robber pawn: name this modern hit!
ahaFactoid: Notice the tiny dots printed under every Catan number token? Five red dots under 6 and 8 literally visualize their 5-in-36 probability per roll!

stem: Invented in a Cincinnati barbershop in 1971 to settle family card arguments, which bright shedding game wrecks friendships with a single Wild Draw Four?
ahaFactoid: Barber Merle Robbins scraped together $8,000 to print 5,000 decks out of his shop—selling the rights a year later for $50,000 plus a dime royalty per deck!

stem: Chrome side lever pulled down to spin three whirling fruit reels of cherries, lemons, and golden bells earned vintage slot machines what outlaw nickname?
ahaFactoid: Even after video slots replaced springs with push-buttons and chips, casinos kept bolting on fake side arms because players love pulling them!

stem: Monte Carlo, 1913: After black landed an absurd 26 roulette spins straight, bettors lost millions piling on red thanks to the classic [ _____ ].
ahaFactoid: The odds of 26 straight blacks are roughly 1 in 67 million—yet on Spin #27, the ivory ball still had zero memory and gave red the exact same sub-50% shot!

stem: At showdown, you flip a trio of Jacks while your rival slaps down two Aces and two Kings—under standard poker odds, which hand scoops the pot?
ahaFactoid: Only 54,912 three-of-a-kind combos exist in five-card poker compared to 123,552 two-pair hands—rarer always rules the felt, so trips beat two pair!

stem: Casino Floor Klaxon! Three of these gambling truths hold up under probability math, while one slick table superstition busts out fast. Spot the myth!
choices: Casino clocks stay rare on walls
ahaFactoid: Casino craps tables force shooters to bounce dice off pyramid-studded rubber backwalls specifically to scramble any thrower’s careful grip or spin!

stem: Rolling twin ones at a craps table draws groans as "snake eyes," while rolling double sixes (1-in-36 odds) earns what rail-yard nickname?
ahaFactoid: Hold two six-pip cubes side by side and those tidy parallel rows of white dots look just like twin freight-train cars rolling down the track!

stem: At a loud Vegas craps table, which foundational wager wins instantly on a come-out roll of 7 or 11 and loses right away on 2, 3, or 12?
ahaFactoid: With a razor-slim 1.41% house edge, the Pass Line lets you root alongside the entire cheering crowd—and unlocks Vegas’s famed zero-edge Free Odds bet!

stem: When a blackjack dealer flips an Ace up-card, they invite players to lay a tempting side wager paying 2-to-1 against dealer 21—what sucker bet is it?
ahaFactoid: Only 16 of 52 cards are ten-valued, making dealer 21 rarer than 2-to-1—handing non-counters a stiff 7%-plus mathematical house edge!

stem: To stop Texas Hold’em players from folding endlessly for free, the two seats left of the dealer button must post forced starter bets before peeking, called what?
ahaFactoid: Called "blinds" because you toss chips in totally blind before seeing hole cards, rising blinds force tournament pros into dramatic duels!

stem: Borrowed from shoving a pinball machine until its pendulum sensor locks the flippers, what short poker phrase means playing wildly after a painful loss?
ahaFactoid: World Series champs admit half of winning poker isn’t card math—it’s resisting emotional tilt when an opponent hits a miraculous two-outer on the river!

stem: Sweeping losing chips off green baize with a long wooden rake while calling "Rien ne va plus!" in Monte Carlo: what French title names this table host?
ahaFactoid: Once referring to a rider seated behind a knight’s saddle ("croupe"), it drifted to gambling aides standing behind high rollers with coins!

stem: Long before Hollywood swapped him into Texas Hold’em, Ian Fleming’s tuxedoed 1953 secret agent James Bond dueled Le Chiffre at high-stakes tables playing what?
ahaFactoid: Bond actually played Chemin de Fer, the classic European baccarat variant where players take turns acting as the Bank and sliding cards from a wooden shoe!

stem: Tile-Rack Triumph: Playing all seven wooden letters off your Scrabble rack in one dazzling turn earns a 50-point bonus universally cheered as a [ _____ ]!
ahaFactoid: Pros memorize high-probability seven-letter "stems" like SATIRE and RETINA because adding almost any seventh letter unlocks an instant 50-point Bingo!

stem: Slim wooden track drilled with 120 peg holes where players chant "fifteen-two, fifteen-four" and score "his nibs" racing to 121: name this pub card classic!
ahaFactoid: Invented by dashing 17th-century poet Sir John Suckling, cribbage’s legendary 29-point perfect hand is so rare—1 in 216,580—that pubs frame players’ names!

stem: Created by Chicago math teacher Charles McNeil in the 1940s so bettors could back lopsided underdogs cleanly, what scoring handicap levels sports matchups?
ahaFactoid: Rather than predicting touchdowns, books adjust spreads simply to balance wagers on both sides and pocket their tidy commission!

stem: Sportsbook Board: Skipping who wins the game altogether, bettors wagering purely on whether both teams’ combined score clears a set tally play the [ _____ ].
ahaFactoid: Weather forecasts move NFL totals faster than star quarterbacks—a 25-mph Lake Erie gale in Buffalo can slash an Over-under line by seven points overnight!

stem: Multiply every possible prize by its exact probability and add them together—in poker and game shows alike, what metric measures a bet’s true long-run worth?
ahaFactoid: A "+EV" call can lose tonight and stay genius—top poker and game-show players judge decisions by expected value, not lucky one-offs!

stem: Playing a European single-zero roulette wheel instead of a Vegas double-zero wheel cuts the casino’s built-in mathematical house edge nearly by what?
ahaFactoid: Dropping that single extra green "00" slot immediately slashes the house advantage from 5.26% down to 2.70%—one of Vegas’s quietest math upgrades!

stem: Trying to break out of Monopoly Jail without paying $50? On any single roll of two fair six-sided dice, your exact odds of throwing doubles are what?
ahaFactoid: Out of 36 equally likely dice combos, exactly 6 are matching pairs (1-1 through 6-6)—so 6/36 simplifies neatly to 1 in 6, or 16.7% per shake!

stem: Buying a 6-of-49 lotto ticket, if you cheekily pick the neat sequence 1-2-3-4-5-6 instead of scrambled numbers, your probability of matching all six balls is what?
ahaFactoid: Every combo holds the exact same 1-in-14M shot—yet skip 1-2-3-4-5-6 anyway, because thousands pick it and would split your jackpot!

stem: Among classic casino-floor games played cleanly with basic strategy, which iconic table game generally hands the player the LOWEST house edge (near 0.5%)?
ahaFactoid: Blackjack rewards sharp basic strategy—though watch the felt, because "6:5 Blackjack" payouts quietly quadruple the casino’s house edge!

stem: Card-Table Klaxon! Three of these blackjack facts are 100% legit, while one angry barstool complaint gets busted by probability math. Spot the myth!
choices: Splits let you play two hands
ahaFactoid: Simulations prove a wild third-base hitter rescues your hand just as often as they "steal" your card—zero long-run harm to your odds!

stem: Game-Night Klaxon! Three of these classic tabletop rules are genuinely printed in the box, while one fierce family house rule isn’t official. Nab the myth!
choices: UNO lets you stack Draw Twos
ahaFactoid: UNO’s official account stunned the internet in 2019 by confirming official rules forbid stacking +2 on +2 or +4 on +4—though house rules remain undefeated!

stem: Chunky six-sided die marked not 1 through 6, but 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, and 64 so players can ratchet up stakes mid-match: which ancient game relies on it?
ahaFactoid: Invented in a 1920s New York club, the doubling cube turned a 5,000-year-old dice race into an electric bluffing duel rivaling high-stakes poker!

stem: Holding four spades after the turn in Texas Hold’em, any of the nine unseen spades left in the deck completes your flush—card sharks call those rescue cards what?
ahaFactoid: A handy felt shortcut called the "Rule of 2 and 4": multiply your outs by 2 with one card left—so 9 flush outs give you right around an 18% river lifeline!

stem: Old-West legend claims all-in gamblers unscrewed wagon-wheel hardware onto the table to prove they couldn’t flee—giving an unbeatable poker hand what nickname?
ahaFactoid: Even if you hold "the nuts" on the Flop, stay sharp—a scary Turn or River card can quietly strip your crown and hand the nuts to somebody else!

stem: Traveling via Yiddish from the Russian word for "winnings," what colorful term (often clipped to three letters) names a bookmaker’s built-in betting fee?
ahaFactoid: Standard -110 odds force you to risk $110 to win $100—meaning you must pick winners better than 52.38% of the time just to outrun the vig and break even!

stem: Game-Show Klaxon! Three of these TV studio realities check out backstage, while one contestant-row rumor flops on the spot. Call out the myth!
ahaFactoid: Bidding $1 on Contestants’ Row is 100% legal—and brilliant game theory whenever you suspect all three earlier bidders overshot the real retail price!

stem: Ticker Wire: Expanded to its permanent headcount back in October 1928, the iconic Dow Jones Industrial Average tracks exactly [ _____ ] major U.S. firms.
ahaFactoid: Not a single one of Charles Dow’s original 1896 dozen remains in the index today—General Electric was the final survivor before exiting in 2018!

stem: Boardroom Blunder, 2000: Blockbuster bosses nearly laughed Netflix’s founders out of Dallas after they offered to sell their DVD mailer for [ _____ ]!
ahaFactoid: Blockbuster went bankrupt a decade later while Netflix roared past $200B—making that Dallas pass one of business’s costliest snubs!

stem: Made permanent after the 2008 banking storm, federal FDIC deposit insurance protects checking and savings accounts per depositor, per insured bank, up to what?
ahaFactoid: Born in 1933 to halt panicked bank runs, the FDIC has never let a single insured depositor lose one penny of covered cash in over ninety years!

stem: Spot the letter and number stamped left of Washington on a $1 bill—they identify which of America’s how many regional Federal Reserve district banks issued it?
ahaFactoid: A-1 stands for Boston, B-2 for New York, all the way to L-12 for San Francisco—check your wallet right now and see where your dollar started its journey!

stem: Soda Revolt, 1985: Buried under 400,000 furious calls and basement hoarders, Coca-Cola surrendered and revived Coca-Cola Classic just [ _____ ] after New Coke!
ahaFactoid: Fans swore it was a stunt, yet Coke boss Donald Keough laughed: "We’re not that dumb, and we’re not that smart!"—and Classic sales soared!

stem: Garage Regret, 1976: Worried about personal debt 12 days after drafting Apple’s partnership papers, third co-founder Ron Wayne sold his [ _____ ] back for $800!
ahaFactoid: Unlike broke twenty-somethings Jobs and Wozniak, 41-year-old Wayne owned a house creditors could seize—and insisted he held zero regrets!

stem: Its own engineer Steve Sasson built the world’s first digital camera in 1975, yet which Rochester film giant shelved it to protect film rolls—and went bust in 2012?
ahaFactoid: Sasson’s toaster-sized prototype took 23 seconds to save a grainy photo onto a cassette tape—execs shrugged, "Cute, just don’t tell anyone about it!"

stem: Long before Mario jumped a single mushroom, which Japanese entertainment titan opened in 1889 crafting hand-painted hanafuda playing cards in Kyoto?
ahaFactoid: Before hitting jackpot gold with arcade cabinets in the late 1970s, Nintendo wildly experimented with taxi fleets, instant rice, and even a plastic vacuum!

stem: Rescuing a "failed" low-tack glue after a choir singer needed hymn bookmarks that peeled off cleanly, which Minnesota firm turned scrap yellow paper into Post-its?
ahaFactoid: Why iconic canary yellow? Pure accident—the neighboring lab simply happened to have leftover canary-yellow scrap pads sitting around for early test runs!

stem: Mailing red-envelope DVDs with zero late fees in 1997 before pivoting into original streaming series in 2013, which disruptor toppled video-rental storefronts?
ahaFactoid: Its very first test parcel was a Patsy Cline CD mailed locally to Reed Hastings’s home just to prove discs wouldn’t snap in postal sorters!

stem: Struggling to pay San Francisco rent in 2007, two designers inflated three vinyl air mattresses and served breakfast to conference guests—birthing what travel giant?
ahaFactoid: When investors passed in 2008, the founders stayed afloat gluing custom "Obama O’s" and "Cap’n McCain’s" cereal boxes and selling them at $40!

stem: Silicon Lexicon: Venture investor Aileen Lee coined the mythical nickname [ _____ ] in 2013 for rare privately held startups valued above $1 billion.
ahaFactoid: In 2013 Lee counted just 39 U.S. unicorns across a full decade—by the 2020s over a thousand joined the herd, forcing analysts to invent $10B "decacorns"!

stem: Wall Street Bell: When a privately owned firm sells shares to everyday investors on a stock exchange for the very first time, it celebrates its [ _____ ].
ahaFactoid: Before IPO morning, founders spend two grueling weeks pitching big funds on a cross-country "roadshow" to gauge Wall Street appetite!

stem: Charging 7,100-pound bronze beast dropped guerrilla-style outside Bowling Green in 1989 by sculptor Arturo Di Modica: it symbolizes what rising stock trend?
ahaFactoid: Di Modica spent $360,000 of his own cash and dropped the bull illegally overnight in 1989—New Yorkers loved it so much the city kept it!

stem: Gleaming brass gong sounded at 9:30 AM Eastern from a marble Broad Street balcony as guests applaud cheering floor brokers: what signal kicks off U.S. trading?
ahaFactoid: Until 1903, NYSE chairmen actually launched trading by whacking a wooden Chinese gong—and today’s brass bell gets rung on camera nearly 500 times a year!

stem: Opening your first paycheck and wondering why the deposit looks slimmer than your salary letter? Taxes and withholdings pare gross pay down to what?
ahaFactoid: Quick memory trick straight from fishing nets: "net" pay is the fish actually trapped inside your net after the tax tide slips back through the mesh!

stem: Wallet Klaxon! Three of these everyday money rules hold up with financial planners, while one tidy-sounding bank tip can actually ding you. Spot the myth!
ahaFactoid: Closing your oldest zero-fee card shrinks available credit and shortens history—often nudging your credit score DOWN instead of up!

stem: Its 1970s Palo Alto lab pioneered the computer mouse, desktop icons, and Ethernet—yet which copier titan famously let Apple and Microsoft commercialize them?
ahaFactoid: After a famous 1979 Xerox PARC tour, a stunned Steve Jobs raced home to build the Macintosh—turning Xerox’s vision into computing history!

stem: Before ruling 1990s pockets with indestructible brick cellphones, which Finnish giant started in 1865 making wood pulp, rubber rain boots, and power cables?
ahaFactoid: Named after the Nokianvirta river beside its first paper mill, Nokia even produced winter car tires right alongside its earliest car phones!

stem: Translating to "Three Stars" in Korean, which consumer-electronics powerhouse began in 1938 as a modest Daegu trading shop exporting dried fish and noodles?
ahaFactoid: Founder Lee Byung-chul started with forty workers selling local groceries—today Samsung builds everything from smartphones and chips to giant cargo ships!

stem: Streaming Flop, 2020: Burning $1.75 billion on celebrity-packed 10-minute phone-only episodes right as commuters stayed home, [ _____ ] folded after six months!
ahaFactoid: Short for "quick bites," Quibi even blocked users from taking screenshots to share memes—starving its pricey shows of word-of-mouth buzz from Day One!

stem: Chrome "horse-collar" grille, push-button steering-wheel gears, and $250M in 1957 hype that flopped overnight: what car became business’s byword for a dud?
ahaFactoid: Named after Henry Ford’s late son despite his family’s protests, the Edsel arrived right into a sharp recession—and became an instant collector’s joke!

stem: Unpainted brushed stainless-steel panels and dramatic gull-wing doors rolled out of Belfast in 1981—what sleek coupe bankrupted its maker before 1985 movie fame?
ahaFactoid: Barely 9,000 DMC-12s ever left the factory before bankruptcy hit in 1982—then *Back to the Future* turned John DeLorean’s flop into pop-culture gold!

stem: Negotiating giant cash severance and stock windfalls triggered if an acquirer buys your firm and shows you the door is nicknamed what in corporate suites?
ahaFactoid: Popularized during the wild 1980s takeover wave, critics mocked golden parachutes for letting ousted CEOs float safely away with tens of millions in cash!

stem: When an aggressive suitor bypasses a company’s resistant board of directors and pitches a buyout offer straight to shareholders, Wall Street calls the raid what?
ahaFactoid: Target boards fight back with medieval-sounding tactics—including "poison pills," "crown-jewel sales," and rescuing "white knights"!

stem: Borrowed from wealthy Broadway patrons who risked their own money backing unproven musicals, what heavenly label names individuals who fund brand-new startups?
ahaFactoid: Unlike big VC funds managing pension billions, angels write personal checks early—like Andy Bechtolsheim’s famous $100k check to Google!

stem: Building a business purely on personal savings and early customer revenue—without taking a dime of outside venture equity or bank loans—is famously called what?
ahaFactoid: Giants like Spanx, Mailchimp, and Craigslist all bootstrapped from scratch—letting founders keep control instead of answering to VC boards!

stem: When a soaring company hands investors four $100 shares in place of every $400 share—leaving total value unchanged while inviting smaller buyers—what move is this?
ahaFactoid: Think of slicing one $20 pizza into eight slices instead of four—you don’t magically gain extra pizza, yet smaller slices make it far easier to trade!

stem: Investing a steady $200 into an index fund every payday regardless of whether markets soar or dip is which calm, automatic wealth-building strategy?
ahaFactoid: When shares dip, your fixed $200 automatically buys MORE shares; when prices spike, it buys fewer—quietly taking guesswork and panic out of timing markets!

stem: Sitting through a dreadful $18 movie or throwing cash at a failing venture purely because you already spent money you can’t recover is what classic mental trap?
ahaFactoid: Britain and France kept funding the money-losing Concorde partly over billions already spent—so economists dubbed it the "Concorde effect"!

stem: Economists note that leaving work for grad school costs far more than tuition—you also give up two years of salary, a hidden trade-off officially called what?
ahaFactoid: Every "yes" hides the cost of its next-best "no"—from skipping wages for school to stuffing cash under a mattress instead of earning 5%!

stem: Glass bell clicking out narrow paper ribbons stamped "GE 94" that New Yorkers later showered from skyscrapers onto astronauts and champs: name this vintage machine!
ahaFactoid: Young Thomas Edison improved the stock ticker in 1869 and earned $40,000—funding the Menlo Park workshop that later birthed light bulbs!

stem: Showing Thomas Jefferson up front and John Trumbull’s Declaration of Independence across the back, which rarely spotted U.S. banknote is still legally printed?
ahaFactoid: Over 1.5 billion $2 bills circulate—most hoarded as lucky charms, though racetrack bettors and Clemson football fans spend them eagerly!

stem: Unlike Wall Street commercial banks owned by outside stockholders chasing profit, a member-owned, not-for-profit savings cooperative is known as what?
ahaFactoid: Because credit unions return profits to their own members instead of outside stockholders, they often beat giant banks on car-loan rates!

stem: Selling a classic car to a stranger, why do smart sellers trust a cashier’s check far more than a personal check? Because payout is guaranteed directly by whom?
ahaFactoid: The bank pulls the cash out of the buyer’s account on the spot and signs the check itself—so a genuine cashier’s check cannot bounce for empty funds!

stem: If a skimmer steals your card number at a gas pump, why do consumer pros prefer swiping a credit card over debit? A debit swipe drains money straight from where?
ahaFactoid: With credit-card fraud, thieves stole the BANK’S money while it investigates—whereas a hacked debit card leaves YOUR real rent cash gone!

stem: Locking in a 30-year fixed-rate home mortgage instead of an adjustable-rate loan buys a homeowner one huge sleep-easy shield—monthly principal-and-interest never does what?
ahaFactoid: Born in the 1930s to replace harsh 5-year balloon loans, America’s 30-year fixed mortgage lets you refinance if rates fall yet blocks hikes!

stem: In 1999, Larry Page and Sergey Brin offered to sell their clean search startup for just $750,000—which now-forgotten web portal famously turned Google down?
ahaFactoid: Excite’s CEO balked even after Vinod Khosla trimmed the tag from $1M—fearing fast search would send visitors OFF his web portal too fast!

stem: Boardroom Klaxon! Three of these wild brand-origin tales are 100% documented history, while one cola conspiracy fails every SEC filing. Spot the myth!
ahaFactoid: Coke and Pepsi have been fierce independent rivals since the 1890s—neither owns the other, yet LEGO really IS Earth’s #1 tiny-tire maker!

stem: Treasury Klaxon! Three of these U.S. currency facts are official Mint and Bureau truth, while one pocket-change scare is pure counterfeit. Catch the myth!
choices: Torn bills lose all cash value
ahaFactoid: If over 50% of a genuine U.S. bill remains—or Treasury labs verify the rest burned—the Bureau of Engraving replaces it free at face value!
